identity.title: Mixture-of-Experts Can Surpass Dense LLMs Under Strictly Equal Resource

problem.claim: Whether MoE language models can outperform dense architectures when total parameters, training compute, and data budget are strictly equal.

gap.claim: This question is described as under-explored despite practical value.

contributions.claim: A perspective and framework for studying MoE versus dense models under equal-resource constraints.
An investigation of MoE architecture leading to an authors-described optimal model design for maximizing performance.
Identification of an activation-rate region in which MoEs can outperform matched dense models, with the region reported as consistent across model sizes.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present their perspective and methodological framework as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that an MoE with activation rate in an optimal region outperforms its dense counterpart under equal total parameters, training compute, and data resources.
The authors report that the optimal activation-rate region remains consistent across different model sizes.
They report extensive validation involving nearly 200 language models at 2B scale, over 50 at 7B scale, and 50 trillion cumulative training tokens.

narrative_sequence.summary: MoEs increase capacity without increasing per-token compute, motivating a strict equal-resource comparison with dense models.
The abstract frames this equal-resource question as under-explored.
The paper proposes a framework and studies MoE architecture to identify an optimal design.
It reports an advantageous activation-rate region, cross-size consistency, data reuse as a response to the data-performance trade-off, and large-scale model training for validation.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns a tightly defined comparison condition with a specific design variable—activation rate—and reports how that variable relates to performance under the condition.

lessons.interpretation: This can make a technical claim easier to evaluate because the comparison regime and proposed explanatory factor are explicit.
lessons.application: When presenting a resource-constrained comparison, define the matched budgets first, then identify the controllable design variable linked to the reported outcome.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the study cannot match the relevant budgets or lacks evidence connecting the design variable to the outcome.

unknowns: The numerical boundaries of the optimal activation-rate region are not given.
The abstract does not specify how data reuse resolves the data-performance trade-off.
Experimental baselines, statistical details, and model-training protocols are unspecified.
Code and models are stated to be released publicly, but no release status or location is provided.
